query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Preheating the build platform during LPBF of AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock will lower thermal gradients during processing, thereby reducing residual thermal stresses, promoting a more homogeneous microstructure, and enhancing mechanical properties relative to conventionally produced high-thermal-load components.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock prepared for LPBF processing
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled build platform preheating step (targeting a temperature window of approximately 300–500 °C) during the LPBF process
generation.conditions: Additively manufacture miniature components (e.g., cubes or thin-walled structures on the order of 1–5 mm in at least one dimension) in an LPBF system under a protective atmosphere; compare components produced with build platform preheating versus those produced under ambient conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced temperature gradients during layer solidification yielding lower residual stresses, minimized crack initiation sites, and a refined, homogeneous microstructure
generation.mechanism: Preheating the build plate reduces the rapid cooling rates and steep thermal gradients inherent in conventional LPBF processes. This moderated cooling allows stress relaxation during solidification, limits the formation of residual tensile stresses, and promotes uniform grain growth, which together improve mechanical performance and reduce processing-induced defects.
generation.predicted_outcome: Components manufactured with platform preheating will exhibit significantly lower residual stress (as measured by methods such as X-ray diffraction), improved mechanical properties (e.g., higher tensile strength, ductility, and hardness), and a more refined microstructure when compared to conventional high-thermal-load LPBF parts.
generation.baseline: Components produced by conventional LPBF processing at ambient build plate temperature, which typically suffer from high residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and microstructural inconsistencies
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable to miniature components processed via LPBF using AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock; the optimal preheating temperature must remain below levels that could induce unwanted phase transitions or excessive oxidation, and the effects may vary with component geometry and specific LPBF parameter settings.
generation.uncertainty: Exact optimal preheating temperature, the degree of stress reduction, and the quantifiable improvement in mechanical properties require experimental validation; interactions with other LPBF parameters may also affect outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of miniature components from the same batch of AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock using LPBF. One set will be processed with the build platform preheated to an optimized temperature within 300–500 °C, while the control set will be processed at ambient build plate temperature. Keep all other LPBF parameters constant across both sets.
measurements: Residual stress analysis via X-ray diffraction or hole-drilling method
Microstructural characterization using SEM/TEM and phase analysis via XRD
Mechanical property evaluation including hardness tests, tensile strength, and ductility measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated samples do not show statistically significant reductions in residual stress and improvements in microstructural uniformity and mechanical properties compared to the control samples, then the hypothesis that platform preheating effectively mitigates the adverse effects of high-thermal-load LPBF conditions on AlCrFeNiSi components is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract An oxygen‐resistant refractory high‐entropy alloy is synthesized in microlattice or bulk form by 3D ink‐extrusion printing, interdiffusion, and silicide coating. Additive manufacturing of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr is implemented by extruding inks containing hydride powders, de‐binding under H 2 , and sintering under vacuum. The sequential decomposition of hydride powders (HfH 2 +NbH+TaH 0.5 +TiH 2 +ZrH 2 ) is followed by in situ X‐ray diffraction. Upon sintering at 1400 °C for 18 h, a nearly fully densified, equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy is synthesized; on slow cooling, both α‐HCP and β‐BCC phases are formed, but on quenching, a metastable single β‐BCC phase is obtained. Printed and sintered HfNbTaTiZr alloys with ≈1 wt.% O shows excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures. Oxidation resistance is achieved by silicide coating via pack cementation. A small‐size lattice‐core sandwich is fabricated and tested with high‐temperature flames to demonstrate the versatility of this sequential approach (printing, sintering, and siliconizing) for high‐temperature, high‐stress applications of refractory high‐entropy alloys. Keywords: additive manufacturing, direct ink writing, oxid

Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.

High entropy or multi principal element alloys are a promising and relatively young concept for designing alloys. The idea of creating alloys without a single main alloying element opens up a wide space for possible new alloy compositions. High entropy alloys based on refractory metals such as W, Mo, Ta or Nb are of interest for future high temperature applications e.g., in the aerospace or chemical industry. However, producing refractory metal high entropy alloys by conventional metallurgical methods remains challenging. For this reason, the feasibility of laser-based additive manufacturing of the refractory metal high entropy alloy W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 by laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) is investigated in the present work. In-situ alloy formation from mixtures of easily available elemental powders is employed to avoid an expensive atomization of pre-alloyed powder. It is shown that PBF-LB/M of W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 is in general possible and that a complete fusion of the powder mixture without a significant number of undissolved particles is achievable by in-situ alloy formation during PBF-LB/M when selecting favorable process parameter combinations.
